content.title: About
content.content: Beets are a root vegetable from the Amaranthaceae family, cultivated worldwide. Cooked beets have a sweet, slightly earthy flavor and a tender yet firm texture. They are commonly used in salads, side dishes, soups, and as an ingredient in baked goods.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beets contain pigments called betacyanins that give them their vivid red color.
Ancient cultures used beet juice as a natural dye for fabrics and foods.
There are over 50 beet varieties, ranging in root color from white to golden‑red.
Cooking beetroot retains most of its nutrients when not over‑cooked.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Betacyanins and other polyphenols help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Nitrate compounds promote blood vessel dilation and improve circulation.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and contributes to a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamin B6, folate, and niacin are involved in energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Beets provide potassium, magnesium, and iron, important for muscle function and blood health.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: High oxalate content may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rarely, some people may experience an allergy to beetroot.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Nitrates can enhance the effect of antihypertensive drugs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked beets can be enjoyed as a side dish, added to salads, smoothies, soups, or used in baking. They pair well with balsamic vinegar, olive oil, nuts, and goat cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked beets in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags to retain flavor and nutrients.

content.title: About
content.content: Blackberries are dark purple-black, juicy fruits of thorny shrubs in the genus Rubus, widely found in temperate regions. They have a sweet and tart flavor and a slightly seedy texture. Blackberries are eaten fresh and used in jams, desserts, baked goods, smoothies, and sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Botanically, a blackberry is an aggregate fruit made of many small drupelets rather than a true berry.
Blackberries grow on thorny canes known as brambles, and wild blackberries are common in hedgerows.
Unlike raspberries, blackberries keep their core when picked.
Blackberries are among the highest-fiber fruits per serving.
They are related to raspberries and roses.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Blackberries are a rich source of fiber, which supports digestion and fullness.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C and vitamin K
items.content: These vitamins support the immune system and normal blood clotting.

items.title: Provides manganese and folate
items.content: These nutrients support metabolism and cell function.

items.title: Contains anthocyanins
items.content: These plant pigments have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Low in sugar
items.content: Blackberries are lower in sugar than many other fruits.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some people may be allergic to blackberries or sensitive to the natural salicylates they contain.

items.title: Possible medication interactions
items.content: Blackberries contain vitamin K. People taking blood thinners should consult a healthcare professional about keeping their intake consistent.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Large amounts of fiber and seeds may cause bloating in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Spoilage and wild berries
items.content: Blackberries spoil quickly, and wild berries should be washed thoroughly and picked away from roadsides and treated areas.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Blackberries can be eaten fresh, added to yogurt, oatmeal, salads, and smoothies, or baked into pies, cobblers, and muffins. They can also be cooked into jams, sauces, and syrups. Wash them gently just before eating.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Blackberries are delicate and should be refrigerated unwashed in a single layer in a breathable container and eaten within two to three days. Discard any moldy berries right away. They can be frozen on a tray and stored in a bag for longer storage.

chicken-thigh-grilled-with-sauce-skin-no.title: Chicken thigh, grilled with sauce, skin not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Skinless chicken thigh, grilled and finished with a flavorful sauce, is a source of high‑quality protein, B‑vitamins, and essential minerals. Grilling locks in juiciness while the sauce adds depth of taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken thighs contain more iron than chicken breast.
Grilling creates a distinctive aroma through Maillard reactions.
Eating the meat without the skin reduces saturated fat intake.
Tomato, yogurt or mustard‑based sauces often accompany chicken, providing additional antioxidants.
Chicken is one of the most affordable protein sources worldwide.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: A 100 g serving provides about 25 g of high‑quality protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Thighs are rich in niacin (B3), vitamin B6 and B12, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The meat supplies iron, zinc and phosphorus, important for blood formation, immunity and bone health.

items.title: Lower fat when skin is removed
items.content: Without the skin, saturated fat content is reduced, making the dish more heart‑friendly.

items.title: Antioxidants in the sauce
items.content: Tomatoes, herbs and spices in the sauce contain lycopene, polyphenols and vitamin C, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium in sauces
items.content: Prepared sauces can be high in salt; choose low‑sodium versions if you have hypertension.

items.title: Cross‑contamination risk
items.content: Chicken can harbor salmonella; ensure it is cooked to an internal temperature of 75 °C.

items.title: Food additives
items.content: Some commercial sauces contain sweeteners, preservatives or artificial flavors that some consumers prefer to avoid.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve sliced grilled thighs in salads, with vegetable sides, or as a sandwich filling. Use the sauce as a dip or drizzle it over the meat before serving. Add fresh herbs, lemon juice or a light mustard for extra brightness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before eating.

egg-white-omelet-scrambled-or-fried-with.title: Egg white, omelet, scrambled, or fried, with cheese and vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of egg white prepared as an omelet, scrambled eggs, or fried, combined with cheese and a variety of vegetables. Egg white is high in protein and virtually fat‑free, while the vegetables and cheese add flavor, nutrients, and texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Egg white is about 90 % water and 10 % protein, with virtually no fat or carbs.
Cheese contributes calcium and vitamin D to the meal.
Vegetables such as spinach, tomatoes, and bell peppers provide antioxidants and fiber.
The dish cooks quickly, making it suitable for breakfast, lunch, or a light dinner.
Egg white is a staple in sports nutrition because of its high‑quality protein.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Egg white supplies all essential amino acids, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The meal is suitable for low‑fat diets, with the main fat source being the cheese, which can be adjusted.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals from vegetables
items.content: Vegetables add vitamin C, vitamin K, folate, and potassium, promoting immune health and heart function.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cheese adds calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Absence of simple carbohydrates makes the dish suitable for blood‑sugar control.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to egg white, experiencing skin reactions or respiratory symptoms.

items.title: Sodium content in cheese
items.content: Choosing high‑salt cheeses can increase sodium intake, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Foodborne infection
items.content: Undercooked egg white may contain Salmonella; ensure thorough cooking.

items.title: Kidney disease considerations
items.content: High protein loads may need to be limited in severe kidney disease.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Whisk the egg white, add chopped vegetables (spinach, tomatoes, bell pepper) and a sprinkle of grated cheese. Cook in a lightly oiled pan: for an omelet, cook until set and golden; for scrambled, stir continuously; for fried, quickly sear both sides.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The dish is best enjoyed fresh. If you need to store it, let it cool to room temperature, then place in an airtight container and refrigerate for up to 24 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Macadamia nuts are the edible seeds of trees of the genus Macadamia, native to the rainforests of eastern Australia. They have a creamy, buttery flavor and a rich, crunchy texture. Today they are grown commercially in Australia, Hawaii, South Africa, and other warm regions, and they are eaten as a snack and used in baking, desserts, and chocolate.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Macadamia nuts are native to Australia and were long eaten by Indigenous Australians.
The shell is extremely hard and needs special equipment to crack.
Macadamias have one of the highest fat contents of any nut, mostly monounsaturated fat.
Macadamia trees can take several years to start producing nuts.
Macadamia nuts are often roasted and sold salted or covered in chocolate.

items.title: Rich in monounsaturated fat
items.content: Macadamias contain mostly monounsaturated fats, which can be part of a heart-friendly diet.

items.title: Provides thiamin and manganese
items.content: These nutrients support energy metabolism and normal bone health.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Macadamias contribute fiber that supports normal digestion.

items.title: Provides magnesium and copper
items.content: These minerals support normal muscle, nerve, and metabolic function.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Macadamias contain flavonoids and other plant compounds with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Macadamia nuts can cause allergic reactions, which may be severe in some people.

items.title: Very high in calories
items.content: Macadamias are very calorie-dense, so only small portions are needed.

items.title: Added salt
items.content: Roasted and salted macadamias can contain a lot of sodium.

items.title: Toxic to dogs
items.content: Macadamia nuts are toxic to dogs, so keep them out of reach of pets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Macadamia nuts can be eaten raw or roasted as a snack, chopped into cookies, cakes, and granola, or added to salads and stir-fries. They can also be ground into butter or used to make plant-based milk and creamy sauces. Choose unsalted nuts when possible.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store macadamia nuts in an airtight container in a cool, dark place. Because of their high oil content, they are best kept in the refrigerator or freezer for longer storage. Discard nuts that smell rancid or taste bitter.

pasta-whole-grain-with-cream-sauce-meat-.title: Whole Grain Pasta with Cream Sauce, Meat and Vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: Whole grain pasta tossed with a creamy sauce, pieces of meat and added vegetables is a balanced dish that combines complex carbohydrates, protein and fiber. The whole‑grain pasta retains bran and germ, boosting its nutritional value compared with refined white pasta.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole grain pasta contains about twice the fiber of regular refined‑flour pasta.
Cream sauces are often made from cream or milk, giving the dish a smooth, rich texture.
Adding meat (commonly chicken or beef) increases iron and vitamin B12 content.
Vegetables such as broccoli, carrots or spinach add vitamins A, C and K.
The tradition of pairing pasta with meat and vegetables comes from Mediterranean cuisine, where such combinations are considered hearty and nutritious.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Whole grain pasta supports regular digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Good source of protein
items.content: Meat provides a complete set of essential amino acids for tissue repair.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Vegetables contribute vitamin C, folate and potassium, while whole grain flour adds magnesium and iron.

items.title: Beneficial fats
items.content: Cream‑based sauce supplies monounsaturated fats that can support heart health when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Broccoli and spinach are rich in antioxidants that help combat free radicals.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The cream sauce and meat make the dish energy‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight management.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Cream in the sauce may cause discomfort for people who are lactose intolerant.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Prepared sauces often contain added salt; choose low‑sodium versions or make the sauce at home.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Whole grain pasta contains gluten and is unsuitable for individuals with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pasta hot, mixing it with the creamy sauce, meat and vegetables. Garnish with fresh herbs, grated Parmesan or a drizzle of olive oil for extra flavor. Pair with a green salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Keep dry whole grain pasta in a cool, dry place in a sealed package for up to 12 months.

peppers-and-onions-cooked-no-added-fat.title: Peppers and onions, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Peppers and onions, cooked without added fat, are a blend of vegetables sautéed dry or roasted. Both vegetables are rich in vitamins, minerals and antioxidants, and the lack of added fat makes the dish low‑calorie.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Red, yellow and green peppers contain more vitamin C than oranges.
Onion is a source of quercetin – a powerful antioxidant that helps reduce inflammation.
Dry‑heat cooking preserves most water‑soluble vitamins, while making some carotenoids more bioavailable.
The combination of pepper and onion intensifies aroma through synergistic volatile compounds.
Vegetables prepared without fat are suitable for calorie‑restricted and low‑fat diets.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system, aids collagen synthesis and improves iron absorption.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Capsaicin in hot peppers and quercetin in onions help combat free radicals.

items.title: Low‑calorie source of fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion, satiety and supports gut microbiota.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Flavonoids and potassium help maintain normal blood pressure and vessel function.

items.title: Provides vitamin A and beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene from red and yellow peppers converts to vitamin A, essential for vision and skin.

items.title: Allergy to onion or pepper
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions such as skin itching, swelling or gastrointestinal symptoms.

items.title: Stomach irritation
items.content: Hot peppers and onions can increase stomach acidity, which may be problematic for gastritis or ulcer patients.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Onions contain fructans that can cause bloating and gas in sensitive people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use the fat‑free peppers and onions in salads, soups, stews, as a taco filling, or as a side dish for meat and fish. They can also be oven‑roasted until lightly caramelized.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cooked mixture in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer keeping, freeze in portion‑sized bags for up to 2 months.

pork-bacon-ns-as-to-fresh-smoked-or-cure.title: Pork Bacon, No Salt, Fresh/Smoked/Cured, Reduced Sodium, Cooked

content.title: About
content.content: Pork bacon is thin slices of pork belly that have been cured, smoked, or dried. This version is formulated with reduced sodium and is ready to eat without further cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional bacon is made from the pork belly, but other cuts can be used.
Smoking imparts a distinctive flavor and extends shelf life.
Reduced sodium is achieved by replacing part of the salt with potassium salts or using osmotic techniques.
Ready‑to‑eat bacon is popular in salads, sandwiches, and as a quick ingredient in many dishes.
In some markets bacon is sold as a “low‑sodium” product to meet health‑focused guidelines.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Bacon provides high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports red blood cell formation and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc contributes to immune function and protein metabolism.

items.title: Reduced sodium
items.content: Lower salt content helps manage blood pressure for those monitoring sodium intake.

items.title: Convenient preparation
items.content: Ready‑to‑eat bacon saves time and is ideal for quick meals.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Bacon contains saturated fats, which should be limited in heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Pork allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic or intolerant to pork products.

items.title: Presence of nitrites
items.content: Smoking may involve nitrites, which can be undesirable in large amounts.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Bacon is calorie‑dense, so portion control is recommended, especially on weight‑loss plans.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Ready bacon can be eaten straight from the package, added to salads, sandwiches, omelets, or used as a flavorful garnish in soups and pastas. For extra crispness, briefly pan‑fry it.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store bacon in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C in its original packaging or an airtight container. Follow the “use‑by” date on the label; after opening, consume within 5‑7 days. When frozen, quality is maintained for up to 2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Potato pancakes are fried patties made from grated potatoes, often combined with onion, eggs and a little flour. The dish is traditional in Slavic, Jewish (latkes) and Eastern European cuisines. Pancakes become crispy on the outside and tender inside, and can be served as a main dish or a side.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: In Russia they are called “draniki”, in Poland “placki ziemniaczane”, and in Israel “latkes”.
They are traditionally prepared for Maslenitsa, the Slavic “farewell to winter” festival.
The classic recipe uses only potatoes, onion, eggs and a small amount of flour, without dairy.
Common toppings include sour cream, applesauce, or fried onions.
A sweet version with sugar and cinnamon is popular in some regions.

items.title: Rich in potassium
items.content: Potatoes are a good source of potassium, which supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Vitamin C
items.content: Cooking retains part of vitamin C, an important antioxidant.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Potato pancakes provide steady energy from slowly digestible carbs.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Grated potatoes keep some fiber, beneficial for digestion.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: When fried in vegetable oil, pancakes contain less saturated fat than many meat snacks.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Frying adds calories; portion control is recommended.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Traditional recipes contain eggs, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: Over‑high heat can create acrylamide, a potential carcinogen; moderate frying temperature is advised.

items.title: Sodium intake
items.content: Salt is often added; people with hypertension should limit usage.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot, typically with sour cream, applesauce, berry sauce, or simply with a pinch of salt. They can be placed in sandwiches, used as a base for appetizers, or served as a side to meat dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked pancakes in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a single layer before transferring to a bag; reheat in the oven to restore crispness.

rice-white-with-dark-green-vegetables-ns.title: White Rice with Dark Green Vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: This dish consists of boiled white rice mixed with dark green vegetables such as broccoli, spinach or green beans. It is rich in carbohydrates, low in fat, and provides vitamins, minerals, and dietary fiber from the vegetables.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White rice is a staple source of energy in many countries.
Dark green vegetables are high in chlorophyll, giving them their characteristic color and antioxidant properties.
The rice‑vegetable combination is common in traditional Asian dishes like vegetable fried rice.
When cooked properly, rice retains most of its starchy carbohydrates while vegetables preserve vitamins C and K.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Rice provides a quick source of glucose needed for maintaining energy levels.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Dark green vegetables supply vitamin K, vitamin C, folate, iron, and calcium.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Vegetables add fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Chlorophyll and other phytochemicals help combat free radicals.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: The dish contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White rice has a high glycemic index, which can cause rapid blood‑sugar spikes in people with diabetes.

items.title: Low protein
items.content: The meal is low in protein, so it should be paired with other protein sources.

items.title: Possible contamination
items.content: Improperly stored rice can harbor Bacillus cereus spores.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot as a side dish or a main course. Add soy sauce, spices, or a drizzle of olive oil for flavor. Pairs well with chicken, fish, or tofu.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked rice in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Keep dry rice in a cool, dry place in a sealed package.

content.title: About
content.content: Soup made with pork or ham is a traditional dish prepared from a meat broth, pieces of pork or ham, vegetables and spices. It has a rich flavor, aromatic profile and a warming effect, often served in colder seasons.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pork soups are popular in Eastern European, Asian and Latin American cuisines.
Ham adds a smoky note that intensifies with long simmering.
The classic Russian rassolnik is often made on a pork broth with salted cucumbers.
Japan’s “tonkatsu ramen” includes a fried pork cutlet in the broth.
Using bones in pork soup increases gelatin content, making the broth thicker.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Pork and ham provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Pork contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The soup supplies thiamine, riboflavin and niacin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Calcium, phosphorus and zinc from bones and meat support bone health and the immune system.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: A warm broth helps maintain fluid balance, especially in cold weather.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Soups are often salted; excess sodium can raise blood pressure.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Ham and fatty pork cuts contain saturated fats, which should be limited in heart disease.

items.title: Pork allergy
items.content: Some individuals may have allergic reactions to pork proteins.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Insufficiently boiled broth may harbor pathogens; ensure it reaches a rolling boil.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the soup hot, often with noodles, rice, potatoes or fresh vegetables. Garnish with herbs, sour cream or a dash of hot sauce to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the soup to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions for up to 2 months. Reheat to a rolling boil before consuming.

content.title: About
content.content: Tamarind drink is a refreshing non‑alcoholic beverage made from the pulp of the tamarind fruit, sugar and water. Tamarind (Tamarindus indica) grows in tropical regions of Africa and Asia, and its tangy‑sweet flavor makes the drink popular in Southeast Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tamarind is often called “the sour plum” because of its distinctive taste.
Tamarind juice is used in cooking as a marinade, seasoning and base for sauces.
Traditional medicine uses tamarind to aid digestion and as a mild laxative.
Tamarind drink is frequently served over ice with lime to enhance its refreshing quality.
The fruit is rich in vitamins B and C, as well as potassium and magnesium.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Tamarind fruit contains polyphenols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Acids and fiber in tamarind promote intestinal motility and may relieve constipation.

items.title: Good source of potassium
items.content: Potassium aids in fluid balance and helps maintain normal blood pressure.

items.title: B‑vitamin content
items.content: Vitamins B1, B2 and B3 participate in energy metabolism and support the nervous system.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Tamarind drink contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Commercial versions often contain added sugar, which can contribute to weight gain and increase diabetes risk.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to tamarind, experiencing skin rash or swelling.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The drink’s acidity may irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Tamarind can affect the action of certain drugs, such as anticoagulants, due to its vitamin K content.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve tamarind drink chilled, often over ice with lime or mint. It can be used as a base for cocktails, smoothies, or culinary recipes, substituting lemon juice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared drink refrigerated at 0 °C–4 °C. Once opened, consume within 3–5 days. Do not store at room temperature for more than a day to prevent fermentation.
